Happy (Copadichromis mloto) is a maternal mouthbrooding cichlid endemic to Lake Malawi, where it inhabits intermediate rocky and sandy substrates. Upon hatching, the prolarvae remain in the buccal cavity of the female, where they subsist on endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic phase. The yolk-sac fry emerge from the mother's mouth after approximately three weeks, at which point they begin exogenous feeding on zooplankton. At this stage of emergence, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.023 grams], a diminutive size that underscores the intense parental investment required to protect such vulnerable offspring. The neonates possess a fully developed swim bladder and commence foraging within days of their first release. The brooding female does not feed during the incubation period, a common energetic constraint among maternal mouthbrooding haplochromines that limits the frequency of successive reproductive bouts. The fry remain in close proximity to the female for several days after initial emergence, seeking refuge in her mouth when threatened, before dispersing into the surrounding habitat as independent juveniles.

As the fry grow and transition through the fingerling stage, their somatic development proceeds steadily under the thermal conditions typical of the lake's surface waters. At a stable water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], individuals attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length at puberty of 10.3 centimeters [Lp = 10.3 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 17.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 17.2 grams]. This size threshold marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, after which males begin to display the characteristic blue head coloration associated with territorial courtship. Females at this length develop enlarged oocytes and become capable of brooding their first clutch. The transition from juvenile to reproductively active adult is accompanied by a shift in feeding behavior, with adults incorporating larger benthic invertebrates into their diet in addition to planktonic prey. Growth rates during this period are influenced by local food availability and the density of competing congeneric species within the rocky littoral zone.

For a mature female Happy, each reproductive event yields a single clutch of approximately 50 eggs [N_R_i = each reproductive event yields a single clutch of approximately 50 eggs], which are fertilized externally during a brief spawning ascent before being collected orally. Under the lake's ambient temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], females typically complete one spawning annually [F_R_i = one spawning annually], a low frequency that reflects the prolonged buccal incubation period of roughly three weeks during which the female fasts. This combination of clutch size and annual spawning frequency yields a relatively modest lifetime reproductive output compared to substrate-spawning cichlids, but the mouthbrooding strategy confers enhanced offspring survival through the vulnerable egg and larval stages. The trade-off between fecundity and parental care is a defining feature of the tribe Haplochromini, and Copadichromis mloto exemplifies this pattern with its limited but well-protected broods. Males, by contrast, are capable of multiple spawning events within a single season as they court successive females, though sperm competition from neighboring territorial males can reduce paternity assurance.

The ultimate total length attained by adults of this species is 13.5 centimeters [Li = 13.5 centimeters], representing the maximum size recorded from extensive trawl surveys conducted in the southeastern arm of Lake Malawi. Reaching this length typically requires two to three years of sustained growth, after which the ultimate wet weight reaches 37.4 grams [Wwi = 37.4 grams]. Individuals at this size are among the larger members of the genus Copadichromis, a group of utaka cichlids known for their planktivorous feeding ecology and the striking nuptial coloration of males during the breeding season. The length-weight relationship derived from field samples follows a power-law curve consistent with the general form established for cichlids in the lake, wherein females tend to be slightly heavier than males of equivalent length due to the mass of ovarian tissue. As the fish approach their asymptotic size, growth decelerates markedly and somatic investment is redirected toward gonadal maintenance and metabolic homeostasis. The maximum body length serves as a useful index for assessing population health and the impacts of selective fishing pressure on this commercially harvested species.

Under the stable thermal regime of Lake Malawi, where surface temperatures remain near 30 °C [T = 30 °C] throughout much of the year, the maximum lifespan for Copadichromis mloto is approximately six years [am = approximately six years]. This longevity is intermediate among Lake Malawi cichlids; it is shorter than that of large predatory species such as Rhamphochromis, but considerably longer than that of small, short-lived mbuna which rarely exceed three years. Senescence in older individuals becomes evident through reduced condition factor, diminished gonadal output, and increased susceptibility to parasites such as the copepod Lernaea. Mark-recapture studies have indicated that mortality rates increase sharply after the fifth year, with very few individuals surviving beyond the six-year mark (6 years) [am = 6 years] at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. The life history strategy of this species balances modest reproductive output with extended reproductive opportunities across multiple breeding seasons, a pattern characteristic of iteroparous cichlids inhabiting relatively stable tropical lake environments where environmental variability is low and adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity.
